Appendix A Near-node scaling of acceptance-weighted, proposal-averaged, and regularized Pulay estimators

In this appendix, we analyze the near-node scaling of several estimators for Pulay-type observables. We first introduce notation and assumptions used throughout this appendix, then derive the variance of the naive estimator, the acceptance-weighted estimator, and the proposal-averaged estimator. We then summarize the asymptotic variance and bias scalings of the various improved estimators, and finally present two illustrative examples, namely a toy model and a time-dependent variational Monte Carlo (tVMC) application, that complement the dense-hydrogen example considered in the main text.

A.1 Nodal surface preliminaries

We consider an observable O⁡(𝐫)O(\mathbf{r}) sampled in VMC from the stationary distribution π⁡(𝐫)=|Ψ⁡(𝐫)|2\pi(\mathbf{r})=|\Psi(\mathbf{r})|^{2}. Throughout this appendix, 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i} denotes the current configuration of the Markov chain and 𝐫f\mathbf{r}_{f} the proposed configuration. Expectations over (𝐫i,𝐫f)(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}) are understood as

⟨⋯⟩=∫d3​𝐫i​π​(𝐫i)​∫d3​𝐫f​p​(𝐫f|𝐫i)​(⋯),\langle\cdots\rangle=\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{i}\pi(\mathbf{r}_{i})\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{f}p(\mathbf{r}_{f}|\mathbf{r}_{i})(\cdots), (48)

where p⁡(𝐫f|𝐫i)p(\mathbf{r}_{f}|\mathbf{r}_{i}) is the proposal distribution. For simplicity, and without loss of generality for the present scaling arguments, we assume a symmetric proposal, p⁡(𝐱|𝐲)=p⁡(𝐲|𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{y})=p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}), so that the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability reduces to

a⁡(𝐫i→𝐫f)=min⁡(1,|Ψ⁡(𝐫f)|2|Ψ⁡(𝐫i)|2).a(\mathbf{r}_{i}\to\mathbf{r}_{f})=\min\left(1,\frac{|\Psi(\mathbf{r}_{f})|^{2}}{|\Psi(\mathbf{r}_{i})|^{2}}\right). (49)

We also assume that p⁡(𝐫f|𝐫i)p(\mathbf{r}_{f}|\mathbf{r}_{i}) is a normalized, local, symmetric proposal kernel that remains finite and non-zero in the vicinity of the nodal surface. Here normalized means that pp is a proper conditional probability density (i.e. ∫d3​𝐫f​p​(𝐫f|𝐫i)=1\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{f}p(\mathbf{r}_{f}|\mathbf{r}_{i})=1), local means that the proposal scale is fixed and does not shrink with the distance to the node or with the cutoff ξc\xi_{c} defined below, and symmetric means that p⁡(𝐱|𝐲)=p⁡(𝐲|𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{y})=p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}), so that the Metropolis-Hastings ratio reduces to the ratio of Born weights. Under these assumptions, the proposal density only contributes finite pre-factors to the asymptotic scalings presented below. We denote the nodal surface as

𝒩={𝐫∈ℝ3​N|Ψ⁡(𝐫)=0}.\mathcal{N}=\{\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{3N}|\Psi(\mathbf{r})=0\}. (50)

Close to a generic point on 𝒩\mathcal{N}, we introduce local coordinates 𝐫=(ξ,𝐫∥)\mathbf{r}=(\xi,\mathbf{r}_{\|}), where ξ∈ℝ\xi\in\mathbb{R} is the signed distance to the node and 𝐫∥∈ℝ3​N−1\mathbf{r}_{\|}\in\mathbb{R}^{3N-1} parameterizes the nodal surface. Assuming the derivative along the normal direction does not vanish, i.e. Φ⁡(𝐫∥)≡∂ξΨ⁡(ξ,𝐫∥)|ξ=0≠0\Phi(\mathbf{r}_{\|})\equiv\partial_{\xi}\Psi(\xi,\mathbf{r}_{\|})|_{\xi=0}\neq 0, a first-order Taylor expansion along that direction gives

Ψ⁡(ξ,𝐫∥)=Φ⁡(𝐫∥)​ξ+𝒪⁡(ξ2),\Psi(\xi,\mathbf{r}_{\|})=\Phi(\mathbf{r}_{\|})\xi+\mathcal{O}(\xi^{2}), (51)

so that

|Ψ⁡(ξ,𝐫∥)|2=|Φ⁡(𝐫∥)|2​ξ2+𝒪⁡(|ξ|3)∼ξ2.|\Psi(\xi,\mathbf{r}_{\|})|^{2}=|\Phi(\mathbf{r}_{\|})|^{2}\xi^{2}+\mathcal{O}(|\xi|^{3})\sim\xi^{2}. (52)

For Pulay-type observables,

O⁡(𝐫)≡(EL​(𝐫)−E)​∂plog⁡Ψ∗​(𝐫),O(\mathbf{r})\equiv(E_{L}(\mathbf{r})-E)\partial_{p}\log\Psi^{*}(\mathbf{r}), (53)

one generically has near the node

EL​(𝐫)∼ξ−1,∂plog⁡Ψ∗​(𝐫)∼ξ−1,O⁡(𝐫)∼ξ−2.E_{L}(\mathbf{r})\sim\xi^{-1},\ \ \partial_{p}\log\Psi^{*}(\mathbf{r})\sim\xi^{-1},\ \ O(\mathbf{r})\sim\xi^{-2}. (54)

Since we are only interested in the leading near-node scaling, and the two sides of the nodal surface differ only by finite prefactors, we restrict the analysis to ξ>0\xi>0. The tangential integrals over 𝐫∥\mathbf{r}_{\|} remain finite and only contribute overall constants, so from now on we keep track only of the normal coordinate ξ>0\xi>0. We denote by ξ0\xi_{0} a fixed microscopic scale delimiting the region where the nodal expansion is valid, and by ξc\xi_{c} (with ξc≪ξ0\xi_{c}\ll\xi_{0}) a formal short-distance cutoff used only to display the divergence of unregularized estimators.

A.2 Naive estimator: power-law divergent variance

For the naive estimator O⁡(𝐫)∼ξ−2O(\mathbf{r})\sim\xi^{-2}, the mean remains finite because

⟨O⟩∼∫0ξ0d​ξ​|Ψ|2​O∼∫0ξ0d​ξ​ξ2​ξ−2,\langle O\rangle\sim\int_{0}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi|\Psi|^{2}O\sim\int_{0}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi\xi^{2}\xi^{-2}, (55)

which is integrable at ξ=0\xi=0. By contrast, the second moment behaves as

⟨O2⟩∼∫ξcξ0d​ξ​ξ2​ξ−4=∫ξcξ0d​ξ​ξ−2=1ξc−1ξ0∼ξc−1.\langle O^{2}\rangle\sim\int_{\xi_{c}}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi\xi^{2}\xi^{-4}=\int_{\xi_{c}}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi\xi^{-2}=\frac{1}{\xi_{c}}-\frac{1}{\xi_{0}}\sim\xi_{c}^{-1}. (56)

Therefore the naive Pulay estimator has a power-law divergent variance,

Var⁡(O)∼ξc−1.\boxed{\mathrm{Var}(O)\sim\xi_{c}^{-1}}\ . (57)

A.3 Acceptance-weighted estimator

The acceptance trick, described in Section III.2, replaces the naive one-point estimator O⁡(𝐫)O(\mathbf{r}) by the conditional two-point estimator

O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f)=a​O​(𝐫f)+(1−a)​O​(𝐫i).\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f})=aO(\mathbf{r}_{f})+(1-a)O(\mathbf{r}_{i}). (58)

This estimator is unbiased, as previously discussed in the main manuscript in the “Acceptance trick” section.

Near the node, the acceptance probability scales as a⁡(𝐫i→𝐫f)∼min⁡(1,ξf2/ξi2)a(\mathbf{r}_{i}\to\mathbf{r}_{f})\sim\min(1,\xi_{f}^{2}/\xi_{i}^{2}). It is therefore natural to split the (ξi,ξf)(\xi_{i},\xi_{f}) plane into the two regions

(A)ξf≥ξi,(B)ξf<ξi.\text{(A)}\quad\xi_{f}\geq\xi_{i},\qquad\text{(B)}\quad\xi_{f}<\xi_{i}. (59)

In region (A), one has a=1a=1, so O~∼O⁡(ξf)∼ξf−2\widetilde{O}\sim O(\xi_{f})\sim\xi_{f}^{-2} and therefore

⟨O~2⟩A∼∫ξcξ0d​ξi​ξi2​∫ξiξ0d​ξf​ξf−4∼∫ξcξ0d​ξi​ξi−1.\langle\widetilde{O}^{2}\rangle_{A}\sim\int_{\xi_{c}}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{2}\int_{\xi_{i}}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{f}\xi_{f}^{-4}\sim\int_{\xi_{c}}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{-1}. (60)

In region (B), one has a∼ξf2/ξi2a\sim\xi_{f}^{2}/\xi_{i}^{2}, hence a​O​(ξf)∼ξi−2aO(\xi_{f})\sim\xi_{i}^{-2} and (1−a)​O​(ξi)∼ξi−2(1-a)O(\xi_{i})\sim\xi_{i}^{-2}, so O~∼ξi−2\widetilde{O}\sim\xi_{i}^{-2}. This gives

⟨O~2⟩B∼∫ξcξ0d​ξi​ξi2​∫0ξid​ξf​ξi−4∼∫ξcξ0d​ξi​ξi−1.\langle\widetilde{O}^{2}\rangle_{B}\sim\int_{\xi_{c}}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{2}\int_{0}^{\xi_{i}}d\xi_{f}\xi_{i}^{-4}\sim\int_{\xi_{c}}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{-1}. (61)

In both regions, we obtain the logarithmic divergence

Var⁡(O~)∼log⁡(ξ0ξc).\boxed{\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O})\sim\log\left(\frac{\xi_{0}}{\xi_{c}}\right)}\ . (62)

Thus the acceptance trick weakens the variance divergence from power-law to logarithmic.

A.3.1 Rao-Blackwell interpretation

In this section, we make explicit the variance-reduction mechanism behind the acceptance-weighted estimator. We first derive the variance inequality stated in the main text in Eq. 30, that is,

Var⁡(O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f))≤Var⁡(O⁡(𝐫i+1)).\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}))\leq\mathrm{Var}(O(\mathbf{r}_{i+1})). (63)

For this, let

X=A​O​(𝐫f)+(1−A)​O​(𝐫i)X=AO(\mathbf{r}_{f})+(1-A)O(\mathbf{r}_{i}) (64)

denote the naive post-acceptance estimator obtained after the Metropolis accept/reject step, where A∈{0,1}A\in\{0,1\} is the Metropolis acceptance indicator and A∼Bernoulli⁡(a)A\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(a). At fixed (𝐫i,𝐫f)(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}), the only remaining randomness is coming from the Bernoulli accept/reject variable AA. The acceptance-weighted estimator is obtained by averaging over this Bernoulli variable while keeping the proposed pair fixed, that is,

O~(𝐫i,𝐫f)=𝔼Bern[X|𝐫i,𝐫f].\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{Bern}}[X|\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}]. (65)

Thus the relevant comparison is between the conditional second moment of XX and the square of its conditional mean O~\widetilde{O}. Since, at fixed (𝐫i,𝐫f)(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}), only AA is random, we can use A2=AA^{2}=A, A⁡(1−A)=0A(1-A)=0 and 𝔼Bern[A|𝐫i,𝐫f]=a\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{Bern}}[A|\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}]=a to obtain

𝔼Bern[X2|𝐫i,𝐫f]=aO(𝐫f)2+(1−a)O(𝐫i)2.\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{Bern}}[X^{2}|\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}]=aO(\mathbf{r}_{f})^{2}+(1-a)O(\mathbf{r}_{i})^{2}. (66)

By contrast,

O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f)2=[a​O​(𝐫f)+(1−a)​O​(𝐫i)]2.\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f})^{2}=[aO(\mathbf{r}_{f})+(1-a)O(\mathbf{r}_{i})]^{2}. (67)

Their difference is

𝔼Bern[X2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{Bern}}[X^{2} |𝐫i,𝐫f]−O~(𝐫i,𝐫f)2\displaystyle|\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}]-\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f})^{2}
=a⁡(1−a)​[O⁡(𝐫f)−O⁡(𝐫i)]2≥0.\displaystyle=a(1-a)[O(\mathbf{r}_{f})-O(\mathbf{r}_{i})]^{2}\geq 0. (68)

This is the local form of the Rao-Blackwell variance reduction, where the acceptance-weighted estimator removes the conditional variance associated with the Bernoulli accept/reject decision. Averaging this (local) identity over proposals gives the global variance inequality stated in the main text in Eq. 30, i.e. Var⁡(O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f))≤Var⁡(O⁡(𝐫i+1))\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}))\leq\mathrm{Var}(O(\mathbf{r}_{i+1})). Alternatively, with the definition of O~\widetilde{O} in Eq. 65, the law of total variance specifies that

Var⁡(X)=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(X|𝐫i,𝐫f)]+Var⁡(O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f)),\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(X|\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f})]+\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f})), (69)

and since the first term is non-negative, Eq. 30 follows.

We now apply this local identity to the near-node scaling. In the region where the proposed point is farther from the node, ξf≥ξi\xi_{f}\geq\xi_{i}, one has a=1a=1 (i.e. region (A), as defined in Eq. 59). The move is therefore accepted deterministically, so X=O~=OX=\widetilde{O}=O pointwise in this region, and there is no conditional “Bernoulli variance” to remove.

The non-trivial reduction occurs when the proposal is closer to the node, ξf<ξi\xi_{f}<\xi_{i}, so 0<a<10<a<1 (i.e. region (B)). In this region, a∼ξf2/ξi2a\sim\xi_{f}^{2}/\xi_{i}^{2}, and the naive post-acceptance estimator has conditional second moment

𝔼Bern[X2|ξi,ξf]∼ξi−4+ξi−2ξf−2.\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{Bern}}[X^{2}|\xi_{i},\xi_{f}]\sim\xi_{i}^{-4}+\xi_{i}^{-2}\xi_{f}^{-2}. (70)

The second term remains singular as ξf→0\xi_{f}\to 0. On the other hand, the acceptance-weighted estimator satisfies

O~(ξi,ξf)2=(𝔼Bern[X|ξi,ξf])2∼ξi−4,\widetilde{O}(\xi_{i},\xi_{f})^{2}=(\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{Bern}}[X|\xi_{i},\xi_{f}])^{2}\sim\xi_{i}^{-4}, (71)

with no remaining ξf−2\xi_{f}^{-2} singularity. The acceptance-weighted estimator can therefore be viewed as a Rao-Blackwell conditional estimator removing variance coming from the Bernoulli proposal (by averaging over it), more specifically removing a “risky” accepted contribution scaling as ξi−2​ξf−2\xi_{i}^{-2}\xi_{f}^{-2}. The logarithmic scaling, derived in Eq. 62, was then obtained by integrating O~2\widetilde{O}^{2} over the two regions of the joint proposal space.

A.4 Proposal-averaged estimator

Starting from the acceptance-weighted estimator O~\widetilde{O}, we define the proposal-averaged estimator

O¯​(𝐫i)=𝔼⁡[O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f)|𝐫i]=∫d3​𝐫f​p​(𝐫f|𝐫i)​O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f).\overline{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i})=\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f})|\mathbf{r}_{i}]=\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}_{f}p(\mathbf{r}_{f}|\mathbf{r}_{i})\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}). (72)

This estimator is unbiased,

𝔼⁡[O¯]=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[O~|𝐫i]]=𝔼⁡[O~]=𝔼⁡[O⁡(𝐫i+1)]=⟨O⟩,\mathbb{E}[\overline{O}]=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{O}|\mathbf{r}_{i}]\right]=\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{O}]=\mathbb{E}[O(\mathbf{r}_{i+1})]=\langle O\rangle, (73)

using the law of total expectation for the second equality. Applying the law of total variance to O~\widetilde{O} conditioned on 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i},

Var⁡(O~)\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O}) =𝔼⁡[Var⁡(O~|𝐫i)]+Var⁡(𝔼⁡[O~|𝐫i])\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O}|\mathbf{r}_{i})]+\mathrm{Var}(\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{O}|\mathbf{r}_{i}])
=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(O~|𝐫i)]+Var⁡(O¯),\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O}|\mathbf{r}_{i})]+\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O}), (74)

we find that O¯\overline{O} is a stricter conditioned estimator than the acceptance one,

Var⁡(O¯)≤Var⁡(O~)≤Var⁡(O⁡(𝐫i+1)).\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O})\leq\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O})\leq\mathrm{Var}(O(\mathbf{r}_{i+1})). (75)

To study the scaling behavior of O~\widetilde{O}, we consider

O¯​(ξi)∼∫0ξ0d​ξf​p​(ξf|ξi)​[a​O​(ξf)+(1−a)​O​(ξi)].\overline{O}(\xi_{i})\sim\int_{0}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{f}p(\xi_{f}|\xi_{i})\Big[aO(\xi_{f})+(1-a)O(\xi_{i})\Big]. (76)

In regions (A) and (B), as defined in the previous section in Eq. 59, we find respectively

O¯A​(ξi)\displaystyle\overline{O}_{A}(\xi_{i}) ∼∫ξiξ0d​ξf​ξf−2∼ξi−1,(ξf≥ξi),\displaystyle\sim\int_{\xi_{i}}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{f}\xi_{f}^{-2}\sim\xi_{i}^{-1},\quad(\xi_{f}\geq\xi_{i}), (77)
O¯B​(ξi)\displaystyle\overline{O}_{B}(\xi_{i}) ∼∫0ξid​ξf​ξi−2∼ξi−1,(ξf<ξi),\displaystyle\sim\int_{0}^{\xi_{i}}d\xi_{f}\xi_{i}^{-2}\sim\xi_{i}^{-1},\quad(\xi_{f}<\xi_{i}), (78)

so O¯​(ξi)∼ξi−1\overline{O}(\xi_{i})\sim\xi_{i}^{-1}. The second moment then scales as

⟨O¯2⟩∼∫0ξ0d​ξi​|Ψ|2​O¯​(ξi)2∼∫0ξ0d​ξi​ξi2​ξi−2∼∫0ξ0d​ξi,\langle\overline{O}^{2}\rangle\sim\int_{0}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{i}|\Psi|^{2}\overline{O}(\xi_{i})^{2}\sim\int_{0}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{2}\xi_{i}^{-2}\sim\int_{0}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{i}, (79)

which is finite. Hence,

Var⁡(O¯)=𝒪⁡(1)\boxed{\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O})=\mathcal{O}(1)} (80)

with no nodal divergence. We have therefore constructed an unbiased estimator with finite variance.

A.4.1 Finite-K approximation

In practice, one may approximate Eq. 72 by drawing KK proposals 𝐫f(k)∼p(⋅|𝐫i)\mathbf{r}_{f}^{(k)}\sim p(\cdot|\mathbf{r}_{i}) and using

O¯K​(𝐫i)=1K​∑k=1KO~​(𝐫i,𝐫f(k)).\overline{O}_{K}(\mathbf{r}_{i})=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}^{(k)}). (81)

This estimator is unbiased since

𝔼⁡[O¯K|𝐫i]=1K​∑k=1K𝔼⁡[O~k|𝐫i]=1K​∑k=1KO¯​(𝐫i)=O¯​(𝐫i),\mathbb{E}[\overline{O}_{K}|\mathbf{r}_{i}]=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{O}_{k}|\mathbf{r}_{i}]=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\overline{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i})=\overline{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i}), (82)

where we defined O~k≡O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f(k))\widetilde{O}_{k}\equiv\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}^{(k)}). The variance then reads

Var⁡(O¯K|𝐫i)\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O}_{K}|\mathbf{r}_{i}) =1K2​∑k=1KVar⁡(O~k|𝐫i)+2K2​∑k<ℓCov⁡(O~k,O~ℓ|𝐫i)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O}_{k}|\mathbf{r}_{i})+\frac{2}{K^{2}}\sum_{k<\ell}\mathrm{Cov}(\widetilde{O}_{k},\widetilde{O}_{\ell}|\mathbf{r}_{i})
=1K​Var​(O~|𝐫i),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O}|\mathbf{r}_{i}), (83)

using the conditional independence of the proposals (and the variance formula for a linear combination of random variables). Applying again the law of total variance, but this time on O¯K\overline{O}_{K} conditioned on 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i}, we get

Var⁡(O¯K)\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O}_{K}) =𝔼⁡[Var⁡(O¯K|𝐫i)]+Var⁡(𝔼⁡[O¯K|𝐫i])\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O}_{K}|\mathbf{r}_{i})\right]+\mathrm{Var}\left(\mathbb{E}[\overline{O}_{K}|\mathbf{r}_{i}]\right)
=1K​𝔼​[Var⁡(O~|𝐫i)]+Var⁡(O¯).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O}|\mathbf{r}_{i})\right]+\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O}). (84)

We can re-arrange 74 into 𝔼⁡[Var⁡(O~|𝐫i)]=Var⁡(O~)−Var⁡(O¯)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O}|\mathbf{r}_{i})]=\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O})-\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O}), and substitute into 84 to find

Var⁡(O¯K)=(1−1K)​Var​(O¯)+1K​Var​(O~).\boxed{\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O}_{K})=\left(1-\frac{1}{K}\right)\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O})+\frac{1}{K}\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O})}\ . (85)

Increasing KK continuously interpolates between the acceptance-weighted estimator (K=1K=1) and the fully proposal-averaged one (K→∞K\to\infty). As consistency checks, one recovers Var⁡(O¯1)=Var⁡(O~)\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O}_{1})=\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{O}) and Var⁡(O¯K)→Var⁡(O¯)\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O}_{K})\to\mathrm{Var}(\overline{O}) as K→∞K\to\infty. The second term is the residual noise from incomplete proposal averaging. Without additional regularization, this residual term inherits the same near-node logarithmic divergence as the acceptance estimator.

A.4.2 Infinite-K limit

Let us allow KK in Eq. 81 to depend on the current configuration 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i}. In particular, one may choose K⁡(𝐫i)∼ξi−αK(\mathbf{r}_{i})\sim\xi_{i}^{-\alpha} with α>0\alpha>0, so that the number of proposals diverges (K→∞K\to\infty) as the nodal surface is approached. This yields a finite-variance estimator while avoiding the uniformly high computational cost of using a large constant KK, independent of 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i}, throughout configuration space.

A.5 Summary of asymptotic scalings

Table 2 summarizes the asymptotic scalings of the variance and bias for the estimators discussed above, together with the regularized estimators O~ϵ(1)\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(1)}, O~ϵ(2)\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(2)}, and O^ϵ\widehat{O}_{\epsilon} introduced in the supplementary material.

Recall that we denote by ξ0\xi_{0} a fixed microscopic scale delimiting the region where the nodal expansion is valid, and by ξc\xi_{c} (with ξc≪ξ0\xi_{c}\ll\xi_{0}) a formal short-distance cutoff used only to display the divergence of unregularized estimators. For the regularized estimators, a simple regularization scheme is to exclude a small region of width ϵ\epsilon around the nodes. In addition, χϵ\chi_{\epsilon} is the smooth cutoff function, mm denotes the number of canceled bias moments of χϵ\chi_{\epsilon}, and KK is the number of proposals used in the finite-KK proposal average.

A.6 Toy model example

To complement the asymptotic near-node analysis, it is useful to consider a minimal two-dimensional toy model in which the nodal geometry is controlled by a single parameter. We therefore consider one particle in two dimensions described by the variational wave function

ψθ​(x,y)=e−2​x2−y2​(x​sin⁡θ+y​cos⁡θ).\psi_{\theta}(x,y)=e^{-2x^{2}-y^{2}}(x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta). (86)

In this toy model, the particle is not subject to any external confinement (i.e. the potential vanishes) so the Hamiltonian contains only the kinetic energy operator, H=−∇2H=-\nabla^{2}. The Gaussian factor localizes the particle and keeps the wave function normalizable, while the linear factor defines a straight nodal line, given by y=−x​tan⁡θy=-x\tan\theta when cos⁡θ≠0\cos\theta\neq 0, so that θ\theta simply rotates the node in the plane.

The quantity of interest is the derivative of the variational energy,

Fθ=d​E​(θ)d​θ=2​(EL−⟨H⟩)​∂log⁡ψθ∂θ,F_{\theta}=\frac{dE(\theta)}{d\theta}=2(E_{L}-\langle H\rangle)\frac{\partial\log\psi_{\theta}}{\partial\theta}, (87)

which is not a physical force since θ\theta is a variational parameter rather than a coordinate of the Hamiltonian, but it provides a Pulay benchmark for the same near-node statistical issues that appear in physical force estimators, given that EL∼ξ−1E_{L}\sim\xi^{-1} and Fθ∼ξ−2F_{\theta}\sim\xi^{-2}, where ξ=x​sin⁡θ+y​cos⁡θ\xi=x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta.

As seen in Fig. 7, this Gaussian toy model clearly exposes the variance reduction obtained from the various estimators proposed in this work. It shows for instance how proposal averaging (K>1)(K>1) improves upon the acceptance-weighted estimator (K=1)(K=1), and how regularizations can be used to further stabilize the results.

A.7 Tail exponents, moment criterion, and toy model example

We formalize in this section how the asymptotic complementary cumulative distribution function (CCDF) exponent is obtained from the near-node scaling of a generic Pulay-type observable. We then show how this exponent, denoted α\alpha, determines whether the nn-th moment of each estimator distribution is finite. The toy model will then serve as an example to visualize the tail scaling of the variance-reduced estimators.

For a random variable XX, we define the CCDF as

Pr(|X|>t)=⟨𝟏{|X|>t}⟩,\mathrm{Pr}(|X|>t)=\left\langle\mathbf{1}_{\{|X|>t\}}\right\rangle, (88)

where 𝟏\mathbf{1} is the indicator function and tt is some fixed tail threshold. Let us focus on the case of interest, where XX is the naive force estimator, denoted FF, which, in terms of the near-node normal coordinate ξ\xi, can be written as

Pr(|F|>t)∼∫0ξ0dξ|Ψ(ξ)|2𝟏{|F(ξ)|>t}.\mathrm{Pr}(|F|>t)\sim\int_{0}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi|\Psi(\xi)|^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{|F(\xi)|>t\}}. (89)

For the naive estimator, F∼ξ−2F\sim\xi^{-2} so the event |F|>t|F|>t is equivalent to ξ<t−1/2\xi<t^{-1/2} and

Pr(|F|>t)∼∫0t−1/2dξξ2∼t−3/2.\mathrm{Pr}(|F|>t)\sim\int_{0}^{t^{-1/2}}d\xi\,\xi^{2}\sim t^{-3/2}. (90)

For the acceptance-weighted estimator F~​(𝐫i,𝐫f)\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}), in region (A) (ξf≥ξi\xi_{f}\geq\xi_{i}), one has F~∼ξf−2\widetilde{F}\sim\xi_{f}^{-2}, hence

PrA(|F~|>t)∼∫0t−1/2dξf∫0ξfdξiξi2∼t−2.\mathrm{Pr}_{A}(|\widetilde{F}|>t)\sim\int_{0}^{t^{-1/2}}d\xi_{f}\int_{0}^{\xi_{f}}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{2}\sim t^{-2}. (91)

Similarly, in region (B) (ξf<ξi\xi_{f}<\xi_{i}), F~∼ξi−2\widetilde{F}\sim\xi_{i}^{-2} so

PrB(|F~|>t)∼∫0t−1/2dξiξi2∫0ξidξf∼t−2,\mathrm{Pr}_{B}(|\widetilde{F}|>t)\sim\int_{0}^{t^{-1/2}}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{2}\int_{0}^{\xi_{i}}d\xi_{f}\sim t^{-2}, (92)

and therefore Pr⁡(|F~|>t)∼t−2\mathrm{Pr}(|\widetilde{F}|>t)\sim t^{-2}. For the proposal-averaged estimator F¯​(ξi)\overline{F}(\xi_{i}), the proposal coordinate has already been integrated out and F¯∼ξi−1\overline{F}\sim\xi_{i}^{-1} (see Eqs. 77 and 78), so |F¯|>t|\overline{F}|>t implies ξi<t−1\xi_{i}<t^{-1} and

Pr⁡(|F¯|>t)∼∫0t−1d​ξi​ξi2∼t−3.\mathrm{Pr}(|\overline{F}|>t)\sim\int_{0}^{t^{-1}}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{2}\sim t^{-3}. (93)

Let us consider a general power-law behavior of the CCDF, that is,

Pr⁡(|X|>t)∼t−α,\mathrm{Pr}(|X|>t)\sim t^{-\alpha}, (94)

with α>0\alpha>0 and for large tt, i.e. t>t0t>t_{0} for some tail onset scale t0t_{0}. From the CCDF definition Pr⁡(|X|>t)=∫t∞f⁡(x)​𝑑x\mathrm{Pr}(|X|>t)=\int_{t}^{\infty}f(x)dx, it follows that the associated tail distribution f⁡(t)f(t) scales as f⁡(t)=−(d/d​t)​Pr​(|X|>t)∼t−α−1f(t)=-(d/dt)\mathrm{Pr}(|X|>t)\sim t^{-\alpha-1}, so the tail contribution to the nn-th moment behaves as

∫t0∞xn​f​(x)​𝑑x∼∫t0∞xn−α−1​𝑑x.\int_{t_{0}}^{\infty}x^{n}f(x)dx\sim\int_{t_{0}}^{\infty}x^{n-\alpha-1}dx. (95)

This integral converges only if the upper limit xn−αx^{n-\alpha} vanishes as x→∞x\to\infty. This requires the exponent n−αn-\alpha to be negative, i.e. n−α<0n-\alpha<0 and so α>n\alpha>n. In particular, the mean (n=1n=1) exists if α>1\alpha>1 and the second moment (n=2n=2) if α>2\alpha>2. Accordingly, this moment criterion (α>n\alpha>n) is consistent with the variance scalings derived above and summarized in Table 3. In particular, for the second moment (n=2n=2), α=3/2\alpha=3/2 implies divergent variance (naive), α=2\alpha=2 is the limit case leading to a logarithmic divergence (acceptance-weighted), and α=3\alpha=3 implies finite variance (proposal-averaged, K→∞K\to\infty). For finite proposal averaging (i.e. 2≤K<∞2\leq K<\infty), the effective tail exponent is expected to lie between the acceptance and infinite-KK scaling limits, i.e. α∈(2,3)\alpha\in(2,3). In that case, the t−2t^{-2} acceptance-like scaling still applies, but its prefactor is reduced by 1/K1/K, so increasing KK shifts the effective tail exponent toward the t−3t^{-3} scaling limit.

As an example, the results in Fig. 8 on the toy model described in Section A.6 illustrate the expected hierarchy of tail softening, with the naive estimator displaying the heaviest tail, the acceptance-weighted estimator (K=1)(K=1) an intermediate behavior, and proposal averaging (K=4,16,64,256)(K=4,16,64,256) yielding the fastest decay. The analysis focuses exclusively on the right tail, as the left tail decays exponentially for θ=0.25\theta=0.25, and therefore does not exhibit heavy-tailed (power-law) behavior.

The fitted exponents α\alpha reported in Fig. 8 are close to the analytical values in Table 3. They were obtained with TREAT [81], a tail-analysis code that estimates power-law exponents from the tails of a sampled distribution. For each estimator, the analysis identifies a lower tail threshold and fits only the data above it. The largest outliers are still included, so the threshold sets the beginning of the fitted tail region without imposing any upper cutoff.

These fitted exponents should be interpreted as finite-sample diagnostics of the analytical near-node scalings. Because the sampled distributions are finite, the tail fit involves a bias-variance tradeoff: if the lower tail threshold is too low, the fit still includes data from the body of the distribution and has not yet reached the asymptotic regime; if it is too high, too few tail samples remain and the estimate becomes noisy. In TREAT, the user typically does not set this threshold directly, but instead specifies an anchor search range from which the analysis selects it. We therefore verified that the reported exponents remain stable under reasonable changes of the anchor range and systematically approach the analytical values as the number of Monte Carlo samples is increased.

A.8 Time-dependent variational Monte Carlo example

As a final example in this appendix, we turn to tVMC, where Pulay-like estimators with formally infinite variance naturally arise in the equations of motion [39, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45]. We follow the benchmark of Appendix E of Ref. [40]: a quench of N=3N=3 particles at unit density, N/L=1N/L=1, on a one-dimensional periodic lattice with L/a=40L/a=40 sites, where aa is the lattice spacing, from the non-interacting ground state (g=0g=0) to a final on-site interaction strength g=8g=8. This benchmark corresponds to a discretized form of the one-dimensional Lieb-Liniger bosonic model [82]. The many-body wave function Φ⁡(l1,l2,…,lN,t)\Phi(l_{1},l_{2},\dots,l_{N},t), with each coordinate li∈𝒍≡{0,a,…,L−a}l_{i}\in\bm{l}\equiv\{0,a,\dots,L-a\}, evolves under the Hamiltonian

Ha​Φ​(𝒍)\displaystyle H_{a}\Phi(\bm{l}) =−ℏ22​m​a2∑i{43[Φ(li−a)+Φ(li+a)]\displaystyle=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2ma^{2}}\sum_{i}\left\{\frac{4}{3}\Big[\Phi(l_{i}-a)+\Phi(l_{i}+a)\Big]\right.
−112[Φ(li−2a)+Φ(li+2a)]−52Φ(𝒍)}\displaystyle\left.-\frac{1}{12}\Big[\Phi(l_{i}-2a)+\Phi(l_{i}+2a)\Big]-\frac{5}{2}\Phi(\bm{l})\right\}
+gaΦ(𝒍)∑i<jδ(li,lj)\displaystyle+\frac{g}{a}\Phi(\bm{l})\sum_{i<j}\delta(l_{i},l_{j}) (96)

where Φ⁡(li−a)≡Φ⁡(l1,…,li−a,…,lN)\Phi(l_{i}-a)\equiv\Phi(l_{1},\dots,l_{i}-a,\dots,l_{N}) (and similarly for Φ\Phi evaluated at the other shifted configurations) and δ⁡(li,lj)\delta(l_{i},l_{j}) is the Kronecker delta. The expressions in curly brackets correspond to the standard fourth-order central-difference approximation to the kinetic term, while the last term represents the discretized two-body contact interaction.

We focus on the time-dependent double occupancy, g2​(0)≡g2​(r=0,t)g_{2}(0)\equiv g_{2}(r=0,t), i.e. the pair-correlation function at zero distance. This quantity is defined as g2​(0)=2​L/(N⁡(N−1))​⟨∑i<jδ⁡(li,lj)/a⟩g_{2}(0)=2L/(N(N-1))\langle\sum_{i<j}\delta(l_{i},l_{j})/a\rangle, corresponding to the contact operator normalized so that the initial non-interacting (delocalized) state satisfies g2​(r=0,t=0)=1g_{2}(r=0,t=0)=1. A simple two-body Jastrow correlation yields a stable long-time evolution, but its limited expressivity introduces a noticeable bias. More flexible parameterizations, such as generalized three-body correlations [40] or neural-network states [83, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45], substantially reduce this bias, but achieving long-time stability becomes much more challenging. Because the matrices entering the tVMC equations of motion are Pulay-like estimators, outliers in their distributions can trigger instabilities in the dynamics. Variance-reduction methods are therefore crucial [77]. Figure 9 shows the resulting improvement from applying the acceptance trick [Eq. 28] in the time evolution of g2​(0)g_{2}(0). Following Ref. [40], we integrate the equations of motion with a fourth-order Runge–Kutta method using a time step d​t=10−3dt=10^{-3}.

Appendix B Near-node scaling of regularized Pulay estimators

In this appendix, we continue the discussion started in Appendix A in the main manuscript, in particular, we analyze the near-node scaling of regularized Pulay-type observables. We will re-use the same notation and assumptions from the first subsection of Appendix A.

B.1 Hard-cutoff regularizations of the acceptance-weighted estimator

Coming back to the acceptance-weighted estimator (though also relevant for the finite-KK proposal-averaged estimator, which has the same variance scaling), a simple way to make the variance finite for any fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is to multiply it by a cutoff that removes a neighborhood of the nodal surface. Two natural choices are

O~ϵ(1)​(𝐫i,𝐫f)=θϵ​(ξi)​O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f),\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(1)}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f})=\theta_{\epsilon}(\xi_{i})\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}), (97)

and

O~ϵ(2)​(𝐫i,𝐫f)=Θϵ​(ξi,ξf)​O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f),\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(2)}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f})=\Theta_{\epsilon}(\xi_{i},\xi_{f})\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}), (98)

where

θϵ​(ξ)={0,0≤ξ<ϵ,1,ξ≥ϵ,Θϵ​(ξi,ξf)={0,0≤ξi<ϵ​and​ 0≤ξf<ϵ,1,otherwise,\theta_{\epsilon}(\xi)=\begin{cases}0,&0\leq\xi<\epsilon,\\ 1,&\xi\geq\epsilon,\end{cases}\qquad\Theta_{\epsilon}(\xi_{i},\xi_{f})=\begin{cases}0,&0\leq\xi_{i}<\epsilon\ \text{and}\ 0\leq\xi_{f}<\epsilon,\\ 1,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (99)

or equivalently, using the step function θϵ​(ξ)\theta_{\epsilon}(\xi) to define Θϵ\Theta_{\epsilon} gives Θϵ​(ξi,ξf)=1−[1−θϵ​(ξi)]​[1−θϵ​(ξf)]\Theta_{\epsilon}(\xi_{i},\xi_{f})=1-[1-\theta_{\epsilon}(\xi_{i})][1-\theta_{\epsilon}(\xi_{f})]. The first excludes all samples whose current point lies within distance ϵ\epsilon of the node. The second is more selective and excludes only proposals for which both the current and proposed points lie in the “nodal square” {0<ξi<ϵ}∪{0<ξf<ϵ}\{0<\xi_{i}<\epsilon\}\cup\{0<\xi_{f}<\epsilon\}.

B.1.1 Variance

For O~ϵ(1)\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(1)}, the lower bound of the ξi\xi_{i} integral is simply shifted from ξc\xi_{c} to ϵ\epsilon, so

Var⁡(O~ϵ(1))∼log⁡(ξ0ϵ).\boxed{\mathrm{Var}\left(\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(1)}\right)\sim\log\left(\frac{\xi_{0}}{\epsilon}\right)}\ . (100)

For O~ϵ(2)\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(2)}, the square 0<ξi<ϵ0<\xi_{i}<\epsilon, 0<ξf<ϵ0<\xi_{f}<\epsilon is excluded. In region (A), the lower bound of the ξf\xi_{f}-integral becomes max⁡(ξi,ϵ)\max(\xi_{i},\epsilon), so

⟨(O~ϵ(2))2⟩A∼∫0ξ0d​ξi​ξi2​∫max⁡(ξi,ϵ)ξ0d​ξf​ξf−4.\langle(\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(2)})^{2}\rangle_{A}\sim\int_{0}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{2}\int_{\max(\xi_{i},\epsilon)}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{f}\xi_{f}^{-4}. (101)

Splitting the outer integral into 0<ξi<ϵ0<\xi_{i}<\epsilon and ϵ<ξi<ξ0\epsilon<\xi_{i}<\xi_{0}, one finds that the former contributes only a finite constant, whereas the latter gives the same logarithm as before. In region (B), the inequality 0<ξf<ξi0<\xi_{f}<\xi_{i} holds. Therefore, if ξi<ϵ\xi_{i}<\epsilon, then necessarily ξf<ϵ\xi_{f}<\epsilon as well, so the pair (ξi,ξf)(\xi_{i},\xi_{f}) lies inside the square removed by Θϵ\Theta_{\epsilon}. Hence the condition Θϵ=1\Theta_{\epsilon}=1 forces ξi>ϵ\xi_{i}>\epsilon, and the contribution from region (B) starts at ϵ\epsilon, yielding once again ∫ϵξ0d​ξi​ξi−1\int_{\epsilon}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{-1}. Hence

Var⁡(O~ϵ(2))∼log⁡(ξ0ϵ).\boxed{\mathrm{Var}\left(\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(2)}\right)\sim\log\left(\frac{\xi_{0}}{\epsilon}\right)}\ . (102)

B.1.2 Bias

For a regularized observable OϵO_{\epsilon}, targeting the associated naive observable OO, we define its bias with respect to the exact expectation value ⟨O⟩\langle O\rangle as

Bias⁡(Oϵ)≡⟨Oϵ⟩−⟨O⟩.\mathrm{Bias}(O_{\epsilon})\equiv\langle O_{\epsilon}\rangle-\langle O\rangle. (103)

Since the (unregularized) acceptance estimator is unbiased, the bias of the hard-cutoff estimators is simply the contribution removed by the cutoff.

For O~ϵ(1)\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(1)}, the contribution removed comes from 0<ξi<ϵ0<\xi_{i}<\epsilon:

Bias⁡(O~ϵ(1))∼∫0ϵd​ξi​ξi2​[∫ξiξ0d​ξf​ξf−2+∫0ξid​ξf​ξi−2].\mathrm{Bias}\left(\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(1)}\right)\sim\int_{0}^{\epsilon}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{2}\left[\int_{\xi_{i}}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{f}\xi_{f}^{-2}+\int_{0}^{\xi_{i}}d\xi_{f}\xi_{i}^{-2}\right]. (104)

The first term corresponds to region (A), where a=1a=1 and O~∼ξf−2\widetilde{O}\sim\xi_{f}^{-2}, while the second corresponds to region (B), where O~∼ξi−2\widetilde{O}\sim\xi_{i}^{-2}. Since ∫ξiξ0d​ξf​ξf−2∼ξi−1\int_{\xi_{i}}^{\xi_{0}}d\xi_{f}\xi_{f}^{-2}\sim\xi_{i}^{-1} and ∫0ξid​ξf​ξi−2∼ξi−1\int_{0}^{\xi_{i}}d\xi_{f}\xi_{i}^{-2}\sim\xi_{i}^{-1}, one finds

Bias⁡(O~ϵ(1))=𝒪⁡(ϵ2).\boxed{\mathrm{Bias}\left(\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(1)}\right)=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2})}\ . (105)

For the more selective cutoff O~ϵ(2)\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(2)}, the removed contribution is restricted to the square 0<ξi<ϵ0<\xi_{i}<\epsilon and 0<ξf<ϵ0<\xi_{f}<\epsilon, so that

Bias⁡(O~ϵ(2))∼∫0ϵd​ξi​ξi2​[∫ξiϵd​ξf​ξf−2+∫0ξid​ξf​ξi−2],\mathrm{Bias}\left(\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(2)}\right)\sim\int_{0}^{\epsilon}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{2}\left[\int_{\xi_{i}}^{\epsilon}d\xi_{f}\xi_{f}^{-2}+\int_{0}^{\xi_{i}}d\xi_{f}\xi_{i}^{-2}\right], (106)

where the first and second terms correspond to regions (A) and (B), respectively. Therefore, both contributions scale as ∫0ϵd​ξi​ξi\int_{0}^{\epsilon}d\xi_{i}\xi_{i}, yielding

Bias⁡(O~ϵ(2))=𝒪⁡(ϵ2),\boxed{\mathrm{Bias}\left(\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(2)}\right)=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2})}\ , (107)

though with a smaller prefactor as compared to O~ϵ(1)\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(1)}, so Bias⁡(O~ϵ(2))<Bias⁡(O~ϵ(1))\mathrm{Bias}(\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(2)})<\mathrm{Bias}(\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(1)}). This is obviously because O~ϵ(1)\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(1)} discards all points with 0<ξi<ϵ0<\xi_{i}<\epsilon, independently of ξf\xi_{f}, excluding the entire strip {0<ξi<ϵ}∪{0<ξf<ξ0}\{0<\xi_{i}<\epsilon\}\cup\{0<\xi_{f}<\xi_{0}\}, while O~ϵ(2)\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(2)} discards “only” the square {0<ξi<ϵ}∪{0<ξf<ϵ}\{0<\xi_{i}<\epsilon\}\cup\{0<\xi_{f}<\epsilon\}.

B.2 Smooth cutoffs and systematic cancellation of the bias

The quadratic bias of a hard cutoff is not fundamental. It arises because the leading contribution removed from the nodal strip is linear in the distance to the node (i.e. Bias∼∫0ϵξ​𝑑ξ∼ϵ2\mathrm{Bias}\sim\int_{0}^{\epsilon}\xi d\xi\sim\epsilon^{2}). This can be changed by replacing the sharp cutoff by a smooth function [34]. We consider

O^ϵ​(𝐫i,𝐫f)=χϵ​(ξi)​O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f),whereχϵ​(ξ)={χ⁡(ξ/ϵ),0≤ξ<ϵ,1,ξ≥ϵ,\widehat{O}_{\epsilon}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f})=\chi_{\epsilon}(\xi_{i})\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}),\qquad\text{where}\qquad\chi_{\epsilon}(\xi)=\begin{cases}\chi(\xi/\epsilon),&0\leq\xi<\epsilon,\\ 1,&\xi\geq\epsilon,\end{cases} (108)

for some function χ:[0,1]→ℝ\chi:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} such that χ⁡(0)=0\chi(0)=0 and χ⁡(1)=1\chi(1)=1. We may additionally impose smooth matching conditions such as χ′​(0)=0\chi^{\prime}(0)=0 and χ′​(1)=0\chi^{\prime}(1)=0. (The generalization to a two-point smooth cutoff estimator O^ϵ(2)​(𝐫i,𝐫f)=φϵ​(ξi,ξf)​O~​(𝐫i,𝐫f)\widehat{O}_{\epsilon}^{(2)}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f})=\varphi_{\epsilon}(\xi_{i},\xi_{f})\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}), for some smooth cutoff function φϵ\varphi_{\epsilon}, will not be pursued here.)

To analyze the bias, we define the following contribution to the mean of the acceptance estimator by

G(ξi)≡∫d𝐫i,∥∫d𝐫f|Ψ(𝐫i)|2p(𝐫f|𝐫i)O~(𝐫i,𝐫f),G(\xi_{i})\equiv\int d\mathbf{r}_{i,\|}\int d\mathbf{r}_{f}|\Psi(\mathbf{r}_{i})|^{2}p(\mathbf{r}_{f}|\mathbf{r}_{i})\widetilde{O}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{f}), (109)

where 𝐫i=(ξi,𝐫i,∥)\mathbf{r}_{i}=(\xi_{i},\mathbf{r}_{i,\|}) and ξi>0\xi_{i}>0. In other words, G⁡(ξi)G(\xi_{i}) is the contribution to the expectation value of the acceptance-weighted estimator after integrating out all tangential coordinates and the proposed configuration 𝐫f\mathbf{r}_{f}, while keeping fixed the normal distance ξi\xi_{i} of the current configuration to the nodal surface.

We saw for the hard-cutoff bias analysis that the contribution removed from the strip scales like ∫0ϵd​ξi​G​(ξi)∼ϵ2\int_{0}^{\epsilon}d\xi_{i}G(\xi_{i})\sim\epsilon^{2}. For that to happen, G⁡(ξi)G(\xi_{i}) itself must scale linearly at leading order, that is, G⁡(ξi)∼ξiG(\xi_{i})\sim\xi_{i}. Assuming GG is smooth enough near ξi=0\xi_{i}=0, its Taylor expansion is

G⁡(ξi)=c1​ξi+c2​ξi2+𝒪⁡(ξi3)=∑n≥1cn​ξin.G(\xi_{i})=c_{1}\xi_{i}+c_{2}\xi_{i}^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\xi_{i}^{3})=\sum_{n\geq 1}c_{n}\xi_{i}^{n}. (110)

The analogous expression of the O~ϵ(1)\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}^{(1)}-bias given in Eq. 104 for the smooth-cutoff estimator O^ϵ\widehat{O}_{\epsilon} is then

Bias⁡(O^ϵ)=∫0ϵd​ξ​[χ⁡(ξ/ϵ)−1]​G​(ξ).\mathrm{Bias}(\widehat{O}_{\epsilon})=\int_{0}^{\epsilon}d\xi[\chi(\xi/\epsilon)-1]G(\xi). (111)

Introducing t=ξ/ϵt=\xi/\epsilon, so d​ξ=ϵ​d​td\xi=\epsilon dt, we obtain

Bias⁡(O^ϵ)\displaystyle\mathrm{Bias}(\widehat{O}_{\epsilon}) =∫0ϵd​ξ​[χ⁡(ξ/ϵ)−1]​[c1​ξ+c2​ξ2+𝒪⁡(ξ3)]\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\epsilon}d\xi\big[\chi(\xi/\epsilon)-1\big]\big[c_{1}\xi+c_{2}\xi^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\xi^{3})\big]
=∑n≥1cn​ϵn+1​∫01d​t​[χ⁡(t)−1]​tn\displaystyle=\sum_{n\geq 1}c_{n}\epsilon^{n+1}\int_{0}^{1}dt[\chi(t)-1]t^{n}
=c1​ϵ2​∫01d​t​[χ⁡(t)−1]​t+c2​ϵ3​∫01d​t​[χ⁡(t)−1]​t2+𝒪⁡(ϵ4).\displaystyle=c_{1}\epsilon^{2}\int_{0}^{1}dt[\chi(t)-1]t+c_{2}\epsilon^{3}\int_{0}^{1}dt[\chi(t)-1]t^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{4}). (112)

Therefore, if χ\chi is chosen such that ∫01d​t​[χ⁡(t)−1]​t=0\int_{0}^{1}dt[\chi(t)-1]t=0, the quadratic term ∼ϵ2\sim\epsilon^{2} vanishes and the leading bias becomes cubic. A simple quartic example is

χ⁡(t)=12​t2−20​t3+9​t4,0≤t≤1,\chi(t)=12t^{2}-20t^{3}+9t^{4},\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1, (113)

which satisfies χ⁡(0)=0\chi(0)=0, χ′​(0)=0\chi^{\prime}(0)=0, χ⁡(1)=1\chi(1)=1, χ′​(1)=0\chi^{\prime}(1)=0, and ∫01d​t​[χ⁡(t)−1]​t=0\int_{0}^{1}dt[\chi(t)-1]t=0. Its bias then scales as

Bias⁡(O^ϵ)=𝒪⁡(ϵ3).\boxed{\mathrm{Bias}(\widehat{O}_{\epsilon})=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})}\ . (114)

Because χϵ​(ξ)\chi_{\epsilon}(\xi) still vanishes at the node and equals 11 outside the ϵ\epsilon-neighborhood, the inner region contributes only a finite constant to the second moment, while the outer region retains the same logarithmic behavior as before, so

Var⁡(O^ϵ)∼log⁡(ξ0ϵ).\boxed{\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{O}_{\epsilon})\sim\log\left(\frac{\xi_{0}}{\epsilon}\right).} (115)

B.3 Polynomial ansatz and higher-order bias cancellation

While the smooth cutoff need not be polynomial (it could be a spline, a trigonometric function or another smooth function), a polynomial ansatz is convenient because all constraints reduce to linear equations for its coefficients so that the bias-cancellation conditions can be imposed analytically. Let

χ⁡(t)=∑j=0daj​tj,0≤t≤1.\chi(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_{j}t^{j},\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1. (116)

If we want the bias to start at order ϵm+2\epsilon^{m+2} (m=1,2,…m=1,2,\dots), then the first mm moments must vanish:

Mn[χ]≡∫01dt[χ(t)−1]tn=0,n=1,…,m.M_{n}[\chi]\equiv\int_{0}^{1}dt[\chi(t)-1]t^{n}=0,\qquad n=1,\dots,m. (117)

Together with endpoint conditions such as

χ⁡(0)=0,χ′​(0)=0,χ⁡(1)=1,χ′​(1)=0,\chi(0)=0,\qquad\chi^{\prime}(0)=0,\qquad\chi(1)=1,\qquad\chi^{\prime}(1)=0, (118)

these constraints define a linear system for the coefficients {aj}\{a_{j}\}. The endpoint conditions give, for example,

a0=0,a1=0,∑j=0daj=1,∑j=1dj​aj=0.a_{0}=0,\qquad a_{1}=0,\qquad\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_{j}=1,\qquad\sum_{j=1}^{d}ja_{j}=0. (119)

Likewise, substituting the polynomial ansatz Eq. 116 into the moment condition Eq. 117 yields

∫01d​t​χ​(t)​tn=∑j=0daj​∫01d​t​tn+j=∑j=0dajn+j+1.\int_{0}^{1}dt\chi(t)t^{n}=\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_{j}\int_{0}^{1}dtt^{n+j}=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\frac{a_{j}}{n+j+1}. (120)

Since

Mn​[χ]=0⇔∫01d​t​χ​(t)​tn=∫01tn​𝑑t=1n+1,M_{n}[\chi]=0\iff\int_{0}^{1}dt\chi(t)t^{n}=\int_{0}^{1}t^{n}dt=\frac{1}{n+1}, (121)

each moment constraint becomes the linear equation

∑j=0dajj+n+1=1n+1,n=1,…,m.\sum_{j=0}^{d}\frac{a_{j}}{j+n+1}=\frac{1}{n+1},\qquad n=1,\dots,m. (122)

Collecting all endpoint and moment conditions gives a matrix equation

A​𝐚=𝐛,A\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{b}, (123)

with 𝐚=(a0,…,ad)T\mathbf{a}=(a_{0},\dots,a_{d})^{T} and 𝐛\mathbf{b} the vector encoding the constraints. If dd is larger than strictly necessary, that is, d+1>Ncd+1>N_{c}, where Nc=m+4N_{c}=m+4 is the total number of constraints, the system is underdetermined and one obtains a family of admissible smooth cutoffs. For the example given in Eq. 113, the matrix AA is square and has a unique solution since a degree-4 polynomial has 5 coefficients and we imposed 5 constraints. In practice, canceling only the leading moment is often already sufficient and provides a good compromise between bias reduction and numerical robustness (as the smooth cutoff becomes increasingly oscillatory (in the interval 0≤t<10\leq t<1) as more moments are canceled).

B.4 Practical choice of the regularization parameter ϵ\epsilon

In practice, the cutoff parameter ϵ\epsilon plays the role of a bias-variance trade-off parameter. As shown above, the smooth-cutoff regularized estimators satisfy

Var⁡(O^ϵ)∼log⁡(ξ0/ϵ),Bias⁡(O^ϵ)∼ϵm+2,\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{O}_{\epsilon})\sim\log(\xi_0/\epsilon),\qquad\mathrm{Bias}(\widehat{O}_{\epsilon})\sim\epsilon^{m+2}, (124)

where, again, mm is the number of canceled bias moments of the cutoff function. The mean-squared error (MSE) therefore behaves as

MSE⁡(ϵ)=Var⁡(O^ϵ)/N⏟statistical error2+Bias​(O^ϵ)2⏟systematic error2∼log⁡(ξ0/ϵ)/N+ϵ2​(m+2),\mathrm{MSE}(\epsilon)=\underbrace{\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{O}_{\epsilon})/N}_{\text{statistical error}^{2}}+\underbrace{\mathrm{Bias}(\widehat{O}_{\epsilon})^{2}}_{\text{systematic error}^{2}}\sim\log(\xi_0/\epsilon)/N+\epsilon^{2(m+2)}, (125)

which shows that decreasing ϵ\epsilon reduces the bias but increases the variance.

In the limit of ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, the estimator approaches the unregularized one and the variance reduction disappears. Conversely, choosing ϵ\epsilon too large suppresses the outliers but introduces a sizeable systematic bias. A practical value of ϵ\epsilon must therefore lie in an intermediate regime where the regularization is “active” but the bias remains negligible compared to the statistical uncertainty. In practice, ϵ\epsilon can be chosen by evaluating the estimator for a small set of (decreasing) ϵ\epsilon values. The optimal region is identified when the mean stabilizes, while the variance remains reduced compared to the unregularized estimator. One then selects ϵ\epsilon as the largest value for which the bias is below the statistical error, while still providing some variance reduction and thus a non-zero fraction of regularized samples.

Appendix C Gradient-to-Laplacian identity

We derive the gradient-to-Laplacian identity used in the main manuscript to obtain improved Hellmann-Feynman force estimators, that we rewrite here for completeness,

2​∂xαv⁡(x)=∇𝐱2[xα​v​(x)]−xαx​f′′​(x),f⁡(x)≡x​v​(x),2\partial_{x_{\alpha}}v(x)=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}\big[x_{\alpha}v(x)\big]-\frac{x_{\alpha}}{x}f^{\prime\prime}(x),\qquad f(x)\equiv xv(x), (126)

valid for x≠0x\neq 0 in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, with x=|𝐱|x=|\mathbf{x}| and for some function v⁡(x)v(x). Using ∂xβxα=δα​β\partial_{x_{\beta}}x_{\alpha}=\delta_{\alpha\beta} and Einstein summation notation, we get

∇𝐱2[xα​v​(x)]\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}\big[x_{\alpha}v(x)\big] =∂xβ∂xβ[xα​v​(x)]\displaystyle=\partial_{x_{\beta}}\partial_{x_{\beta}}\big[x_{\alpha}v(x)\big]
=∂xβ(δα​β​v​(x)+xα​∂xβv⁡(x))\displaystyle=\partial_{x_{\beta}}\left(\delta_{\alpha\beta}v(x)+x_{\alpha}\partial_{x_{\beta}}v(x)\right)
=∂xαv⁡(x)+∂xβ[xα​∂xβv⁡(x)]\displaystyle=\partial_{x_{\alpha}}v(x)+\partial_{x_{\beta}}\big[x_{\alpha}\partial_{x_{\beta}}v(x)\big]
=∂xαv⁡(x)+δα​β​∂xβv⁡(x)+xα​∂xβ∂xβv⁡(x)\displaystyle=\partial_{x_{\alpha}}v(x)+\delta_{\alpha\beta}\partial_{x_{\beta}}v(x)+x_{\alpha}\partial_{x_{\beta}}\partial_{x_{\beta}}v(x)
=2​∂xαv⁡(x)+xα​∇𝐱2v​(x).\displaystyle=2\partial_{x_{\alpha}}v(x)+x_{\alpha}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}v(x). (127)

The radial Laplacian (in three-dimension) is derived as follows

∇𝐱v​(x)\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}v(x) =v′​(x)​∇𝐱x=v′​(x)​𝐱x,\displaystyle=v^{\prime}(x)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}x=v^{\prime}(x)\frac{\mathbf{x}}{x}, (128)
∇𝐱2​v​(x)\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}v(x) =∇𝐱⋅(v′​(x)​𝐱x)=∇𝐱v′​(x)⋅𝐱x+v′​(x)​∇𝐱⋅(𝐱x)=v′′​(x)+2x​v′​(x),\displaystyle=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\cdot\left(v^{\prime}(x)\frac{\mathbf{x}}{x}\right)=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}v^{\prime}(x)\cdot\frac{\mathbf{x}}{x}+v^{\prime}(x)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\cdot\left(\frac{\mathbf{x}}{x}\right)=v^{\prime\prime}(x)+\frac{2}{x}v^{\prime}(x), (129)

where we used ∇𝐱v′​(x)=v′′​(x)​𝐱/x\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}v^{\prime}(x)=v^{\prime\prime}(x)\mathbf{x}/x and ∇𝐱⋅(𝐱/x)=(∇𝐱⋅𝐱)/x+𝐱⋅∇𝐱(1/x)=3/x−1/x=2/x\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\cdot(\mathbf{x}/x)=(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\cdot\mathbf{x})/x+\mathbf{x}\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}(1/x)=3/x-1/x=2/x (since ∇𝐱(1/x)=−𝐱/x3\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}(1/x)=-\mathbf{x}/x^{3}). Now introduce f⁡(x)=x​v​(x)f(x)=xv(x). A direct differentiation gives

f′′​(x)=d2d​x2​[x​v​(x)]=dd​x​[v⁡(x)+x​v′​(x)]=2​v′​(x)+x​v′′​(x),f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{d^{2}}{dx^{2}}\big[xv(x)\big]=\frac{d}{dx}\big[v(x)+xv^{\prime}(x)\big]=2v^{\prime}(x)+xv^{\prime\prime}(x), (130)

so Eq. 129 can be written as

∇𝐱2​v​(x)=1x​f′′​(x).\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}v(x)=\frac{1}{x}f^{\prime\prime}(x). (131)

Substituting Eq. 131 into 127 yields

∇𝐱2[xα​v​(x)]=2​∂xαv⁡(x)+xαx​f′′​(x),\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}\big[x_{\alpha}v(x)\big]=2\partial_{x_{\alpha}}v(x)+\frac{x_{\alpha}}{x}f^{\prime\prime}(x), (132)

which rearranges to Eq. 126.

Appendix D Divergence theorem identities

We adopt in this appendix a more math-based notation, in particular without putting vectors in bold font. Let x∈Ωx\in\Omega denote a configuration-space sample (e.g. x≡𝐫∈ℝ3​Nx\equiv\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{3N} in VMC), with domain Ω=ℝd\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{d} for open boundary conditions, or a periodic simulation cell under periodic boundary conditions. Let π⁡(x)≥0\pi(x)\geq 0 be an unnormalized probability distribution on Ω\Omega, with normalization Z=∫Ωπ⁡(x)​𝑑xZ=\int_{\Omega}\pi(x)dx. For an observable OO, we write ⟨O⟩≡⟨O⟩π=Z−1​∫ΩO⁡(x)​π​(x)​𝑑x\langle O\rangle\equiv\langle O\rangle_{\pi}=Z^{-1}\int_{\Omega}O(x)\pi(x)dx. For a sufficiently regular vector field A:Ω→ℝdA:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, define the Langevin Stein operator [61]

ℒπ​[A]​(x)≡∇⋅A⁡(x)+A⁡(x)⋅∇log⁡π​(x),\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A](x)\equiv\nabla\cdot A(x)+A(x)\cdot\nabla\log\pi(x), (133)

where ∇≡∇x\nabla\equiv\nabla_{x} is the configuration-space gradient. Throughout this section, we assume boundary conditions such that the divergence theorem can be applied to the vector field entering each identity without producing residual boundary terms. Concretely, for open boundary conditions, it means that the relevant field π⁡(x)​A​(x)​H​(x)\pi(x)A(x)H(x), defined below for some indicator function HH, decays sufficiently rapidly as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty, while for periodic boundary conditions, π⁡(x),A⁡(x)\pi(x),A(x) and H⁡(x)H(x) are periodic on Ω\Omega. In each subsection below, we present an identity with an associated (boxed) example.

D.1 Codimension-0: zero-mean control variate

Consider the vector field

F⁡(x)=π⁡(x)​A​(x).F(x)=\pi(x)A(x). (134)

By the divergence theorem and the above boundary assumptions,

∫Ω∇⋅F⁡(x)​𝑑x=∫∂ΩF⋅n​𝑑S=0.\int_{\Omega}\nabla\cdot F(x)dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot ndS=0. (135)

Using ∇⋅(π​A)=π⁡(∇⋅A+A⋅∇log⁡π)=π​ℒπ​[A]\nabla\cdot(\pi A)=\pi(\nabla\cdot A+A\cdot\nabla\log\pi)=\pi\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A], we obtain ⟨ℒπ​[A]⟩=0\langle\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]\rangle=0, so for any observable OO,

⟨O⟩=⟨O+ℒπ​[A]⟩.\boxed{\langle O\rangle=\langle O+\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]\rangle}\ . (136)

Thus ℒπ​[A]\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A] is a zero-mean control variate correction, which can reduce the estimator variance when the vector field AA is chosen appropriately.

D.2 Codimension-1: surface-to-volume conversion

Let ξ:Ω→ℝ\xi:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} be differentiable, fix s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, and define the Heaviside step function θs​(x)≡θ⁡(s−ξ⁡(x))\theta_{s}(x)\equiv\theta(s-\xi(x)), which should be periodized accordingly under periodic boundary conditions. Consider the truncated vector field

F⁡(x)=π⁡(x)​θs​(x)​A​(x).F(x)=\pi(x)\theta_{s}(x)A(x). (140)

Applying the divergence theorem on Ω\Omega gives, as before, ∫Ω∇⋅F​𝑑x=0\int_{\Omega}\nabla\cdot Fdx=0. Expanding ∇⋅F=∇⋅(π​θs​A)\nabla\cdot F=\nabla\cdot(\pi\theta_{s}A) via the product rule yields

∇⋅(π​θs​A)=π​θs​ℒπ​[A]+π⁡(∇θs)⋅A.\nabla\cdot(\pi\theta_{s}A)=\pi\theta_{s}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]+\pi(\nabla\theta_{s})\cdot A. (141)

Using ∇θs=∇xθ(s−ξ(x))=−δ(s−ξ)∇ξ\nabla\theta_{s}=\nabla_{x}\theta(s-\xi(x))=-\delta(s-\xi)\nabla\xi (since ∂tθ⁡(t)=δ⁡(t)\partial_{t}\theta(t)=\delta(t)), we obtain the identity

⟨δ⁡(s−ξ)​A⋅∇ξ⟩=⟨θs​ℒπ​[A]⟩.\boxed{\langle\delta(s-\xi)A\cdot\nabla\xi\rangle=\langle\theta_{s}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]\rangle}\ . (142)

For observables involving a single delta function of the form ⟨δ⁡(s−ξ⁡(x))​W​(x)⟩\langle\delta(s-\xi(x))W(x)\rangle (e.g. (multipole) densities, pair correlations, angular distributions), one typically chooses AA such that on {ξ=s}\{\xi=s\}, A⁡(x,s)⋅∇ξ​(x)=W⁡(x)A(x;s)\cdot\nabla\xi(x)=W(x). A simple choice is

A⁡(x,s)=W⁡(x)​∇ξ​(x)|∇ξ​(x)|2,\boxed{A(x;s)=W(x)\frac{\nabla\xi(x)}{|\nabla\xi(x)|^{2}}}\ , (143)

provided ∇ξ≠0\nabla\xi\neq 0. With this choice, the left-hand side of Eq. 142 reduces to ⟨δ⁡(s−ξ)​W⟩\langle\delta(s-\xi)W\rangle, while the right-hand side is a sublevel-set (volume) average over {ξ≤s}\{\xi\leq s\}. We emphasize that Eq. 142 turns an integration over a shell into an integration over a ball, therefore increasing the signal-to-noise ratio in numerical calculations.

D.3 Codimension-2: intersection-to-volume conversion

We now consider observables involving two delta constraints of the generic form

g⁡(s,t)=⟨δ⁡(s−ξ⁡(x))​δ​(t−η⁡(x))⟩,g(s,t)=\big\langle\delta(s-\xi(x))\delta(t-\eta(x))\big\rangle, (148)

for differentiable function ξ,η:Ω→ℝ\xi,\eta:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} and constants s,t∈ℝs,t\in\mathbb{R}. These estimators are supported on the intersection {ξ=s}∩{η=t}\{\xi=s\}\cap\{\eta=t\}. Define

θs​(x)≡θ⁡(s−ξ⁡(x)),θt​(x)≡θ⁡(t−η⁡(x)),δs​(x)=δ⁡(s−ξ⁡(x)),δt​(x)≡δ⁡(t−η⁡(x)),\theta_{s}(x)\equiv\theta(s-\xi(x)),\qquad\theta_{t}(x)\equiv\theta(t-\eta(x)),\qquad\delta_{s}(x)=\delta(s-\xi(x)),\qquad\delta_{t}(x)\equiv\delta(t-\eta(x)), (149)

and let p=∇ξp=\nabla\xi, q=∇ηq=\nabla\eta, so that ∇θs=−δs​p\nabla\theta_{s}=-\delta_{s}p and ∇θt=−δt​q\nabla\theta_{t}=-\delta_{t}q.

First elimination. Applying the divergence theorem to the doubly truncated vector field

FA​(x)=π⁡(x)​θs​(x)​θt​(x)​A​(x),F_{A}(x)=\pi(x)\theta_{s}(x)\theta_{t}(x)A(x), (150)

yields ∫Ω∇⋅FA​𝑑x=0\int_{\Omega}\nabla\cdot F_{A}dx=0, given our initial boundary assumptions. Expanding gives

∇⋅(π​θs​θt​A)=π​θs​θt​ℒπ​[A]−π​δs​θt​(A⋅p)−π​θs​δt​(A⋅q).\nabla\cdot(\pi\theta_{s}\theta_{t}A)=\pi\theta_{s}\theta_{t}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]-\pi\delta_{s}\theta_{t}(A\cdot p)-\pi\theta_{s}\delta_{t}(A\cdot q). (151)

To eliminate one surface term, without loss of generality, we choose AA such that (we will come back to this choice later, causing asymmetry in the final expression)

A⋅p=1andA⋅q=0.A\cdot p=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad A\cdot q=0. (152)

In that case, integrating over Ω\Omega and dividing by the normalization ZZ, we get

⟨δs​θt⟩=⟨θs​θt​ℒπ​[A]⟩.\langle\delta_{s}\theta_{t}\rangle=\langle\theta_{s}\theta_{t}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]\rangle. (153)

We now differentiate this expression with respect to tt, noting that AA and ℒπ​[A]\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A] are independent of tt, to reach the intermediate expression

⟨δs​δt⟩=⟨θs​δt​ℒπ​[A]⟩.\langle\delta_{s}\delta_{t}\rangle=\langle\theta_{s}\delta_{t}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]\rangle. (154)

Second elimination. As we are still left with one delta function on the right-hand side of Eq. 154, we proceed to eliminate it by applying a second time the divergence theorem, but this time to the new vector field (defined in such a way to be able to use the intermediate identity Eq. 154)

FB​(x)=π⁡(x)​θs​(x)​θt​(x)​B​(x)​ℒπ​[A]​(x).F_{B}(x)=\pi(x)\theta_{s}(x)\theta_{t}(x)B(x)\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A](x). (155)

Applying the divergence theorem to FBF_{B} gives ∫Ω∇⋅FB​𝑑x=0\int_{\Omega}\nabla\cdot F_{B}dx=0. Expanding again using the product rule, we get two volume and two surface terms

∇⋅(π​θs​θt​B​ℒπ​[A])=π​θs​θt​{ℒπ​[B]​ℒπ​[A]+B⋅∇ℒπ​[A]}−π⁡{δs​θt​(B⋅p)+θs​δt​(B⋅q)}​ℒπ​[A].\nabla\cdot(\pi\theta_{s}\theta_{t}B\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A])=\pi\theta_{s}\theta_{t}\Big\{\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[B]\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]+B\cdot\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]\Big\}-\pi\Big\{\delta_{s}\theta_{t}(B\cdot p)+\theta_{s}\delta_{t}(B\cdot q)\Big\}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]. (156)

To be able to use the identity given in Eq. 154, we choose BB such that

B⋅p=0andB⋅q=1.B\cdot p=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad B\cdot q=1. (157)

Applying these constraints, integrating over Ω\Omega and dividing by ZZ, we get

⟨θs​δt​ℒπ​[A]⟩=⟨θs​θt​(ℒπ​[B]​ℒπ​[A]+B⋅∇ℒπ​[A])⟩.\langle\theta_{s}\delta_{t}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]\rangle=\langle\theta_{s}\theta_{t}(\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[B]\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]+B\cdot\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A])\rangle. (158)

We can finally combine Eqs. 154 and 158 to obtain an expression that is now free of delta functions, that is,

⟨δs​δt⟩=⟨θs​θt​(ℒπ​[B]​ℒπ​[A]+B⋅∇ℒπ​[A])⟩.\langle\delta_{s}\delta_{t}\rangle=\langle\theta_{s}\theta_{t}(\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[B]\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]+B\cdot\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A])\rangle. (159)

Given that we eliminated the two delta functions sequentially, the expression is manifestly asymmetric, as previously alluded to. This can be mathematically seen even better by writing the expression in parentheses as ℒπ​[B]​ℒπ​[A]+B⋅∇ℒπ​[A]=ℒπ​[B​ℒπ​[A]]\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[B]\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]+B\cdot\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]=\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[B\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]], the latter clearly identifying that BB was introduced after weighting by ℒπ​[A]\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]. If instead δt\delta_{t} is first removed with BB and then δs\delta_{s} is removed with AA, the two theta functions would be multiplied by ℒπ​[A​ℒπ​[B]]\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[B]] instead of ℒπ​[B​ℒπ​[A]]\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[B\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]]. We can therefore average the two orderings to obtain the symmetric formula

⟨δs​δt⟩=⟨θs​θt​12​(ℒπ​[A​ℒπ​[B]]+ℒπ​[B​ℒπ​[A]])⟩,\boxed{\langle\delta_{s}\delta_{t}\rangle=\left\langle\theta_{s}\theta_{t}\frac{1}{2}(\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[B]]+\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[B\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]])\right\rangle}\ , (160)

which is now indeed manifestly symmetric under swapping (A,ξ,s)↔(B,η,t)(A,\xi,s)\leftrightarrow(B,\eta,t). In addition, one can use the identity ℒπ​[ϕ​A]=ℒπ​[A]​ϕ+A⋅∇ϕ\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[\phi A]=\mathcal{L}_{\pi}[A]\phi+A\cdot\nabla\phi, for some scalar ϕ\phi, to expand this expression (and facilitate computer implementation).

Constructing the vector fields AA and BB. We started with the level-set constraints ξ⁡(x)=s\xi(x)=s and η⁡(x)=t\eta(x)=t, and denoted their gradients by p=∇ξp=\nabla\xi and q=∇ηq=\nabla\eta, which (when linearly independent) span the 2D normal subspace associated with the two constraints in configuration space. The only requirements that define AA and BB, given in Eqs. 152 and 157, are dot products with pp and qq. It is therefore a natural choice to take AA and BB to be inside span⁡({p,q})\mathrm{span}(\{p,q\}) (in particular, neglecting tangent components to both constraints), meaning that

A=a​p+b​qandB=c​p+d​q,A=ap+bq\qquad\text{and}\qquad B=cp+dq, (161)

for a,b,c,d∈ℝa,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}. Substituting first this form of AA into the dot product constraints given in Eq. 152 gives the following two equations

(a​p+b​q)⋅p=a⁡(p⋅p)+b⁡(q⋅p)=1,\displaystyle(ap+bq)\cdot p=a(p\cdot p)+b(q\cdot p)=1, (162)
(a​p+b​q)⋅q=a⁡(p⋅q)+b⁡(q⋅q)=0,\displaystyle(ap+bq)\cdot q=a(p\cdot q)+b(q\cdot q)=0, (163)

which in matrix form reads

G​(ab)=(10),G=(p⋅pq⋅pp⋅qq⋅q),G\begin{pmatrix}a\\ b\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\quad G=\begin{pmatrix}p\cdot p&q\cdot p\\ p\cdot q&q\cdot q\end{pmatrix}, (165)

where GG is the Gram matrix. Solving for the coefficients

(ab)=G−1​(10),G−1=1|G|​(q⋅q−q⋅p−p⋅qp⋅p),\begin{pmatrix}a\\ b\end{pmatrix}=G^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\quad G^{-1}=\frac{1}{|G|}\begin{pmatrix}q\cdot q&-q\cdot p\\ -p\cdot q&p\cdot p\end{pmatrix}, (166)

where |G|=det⁡(G)=(p⋅p)​(q⋅q)−(p⋅q)2|G|=\mathrm{det}(G)=(p\cdot p)(q\cdot q)-(p\cdot q)^{2}, we obtain

A=(q⋅q)​p−(p⋅q)​q|G|.\boxed{A=\frac{(q\cdot q)p-(p\cdot q)q}{|G|}}\ . (167)

Proceeding similarly for BB, using Eq. 157, we obtain

B=−(q⋅p)​p+(p⋅p)​q|G|.\boxed{B=\frac{-(q\cdot p)p+(p\cdot p)q}{|G|}}\ . (168)

Selecting AA to satisfy A⋅p=1A\cdot p=1 and A⋅q=0A\cdot q=0 makes AA have unit flux through the ξ\xi-level set while remaining tangent to the η\eta-level set, while selecting BB with B⋅p=0B\cdot p=0 and B⋅q=1B\cdot q=1 enforces the complementary property. This is essential because a single application of the divergence theorem produces codimension-1 boundary terms, while the dual constraints imposed isolate the desired boundary (intersection) contribution.

Higher codimension. The procedure obviously generalizes to observables with kk-delta functions, of the form

g⁡(𝐬)=⟨∏a=1kδ⁡(sa−ξa​(x))⟩,g(\mathbf{s})=\left\langle\prod_{a=1}^{k}\delta(s_{a}-\xi_{a}(x))\right\rangle, (169)

where the gradients pa=∇ξa∈ℝdp_{a}=\nabla\xi_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} can be defined. However, eliminating delta functions sequentially increases the highest derivative order in the estimator linearly with kk, which quickly becomes impractical as kk grows. A compromise would be to eliminate one (or a few) delta functions analytically and treat the remaining variables with the usual binning or kernel smoothing approaches.

Appendix E Periodic alternative for the 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-function

In this section, we present the estimator proposed by Qian et al. [25] that we compared with in the main manuscript, in the figure comparing various Hellmann-Feynman force estimators. Instead of providing an explicit expression for the 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-function (as we do in the main text), the authors implicitly define 𝐐\mathbf{Q} by providing an expression for its gradient. The expression reads as follows

∂i​αQI​β=−∑𝐓ZI[erfc⁡(κ​ri​I​𝐓)ri​I​𝐓3ri​I​𝐓,βri​I​𝐓,α−δα​βerfc⁡(κ​ri​I​𝐓)ri​I​𝐓−δα​βκπEi(−κ2ri​I​𝐓2)],\partial_{i\alpha}Q_{I\beta}=-\sum_{\mathbf{T}}Z_{I}\left[\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\kappa r_{iI\mathbf{T}})}{r_{iI\mathbf{T}}^{3}}r_{iI\mathbf{T},\beta}r_{iI\mathbf{T},\alpha}-\delta_{\alpha\beta}\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\kappa r_{iI\mathbf{T}})}{r_{iI\mathbf{T}}}-\delta_{\alpha\beta}\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{\pi}}\mathrm{Ei}(-\kappa^{2}r_{iI\mathbf{T}}^{2})\right], (171)

where ri​I​𝐓≡|𝐫i−𝐑I−𝐓|r_{iI\mathbf{T}}\equiv|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}-\mathbf{T}|, ∂i​α≡∂/∂ri​α\partial_{i\alpha}\equiv\partial/\partial r_{i\alpha}, and α,β∈{x,y,z}\alpha,\beta\in\{x,y,z\}. In vector form, the gradient of the xx-component, for example, can be written explicitly as

∇iQI​x=−∑𝐓ZI(erfc⁡(κ​ri​I​𝐓)​ri​I​𝐓,x2ri​I​𝐓3−erfc⁡(κ​ri​I​𝐓)ri​I​𝐓−κπ​Ei​(−κ2​ri​I​𝐓2)erfc⁡(κ​ri​I​𝐓)​ri​I​𝐓,x​ri​I​𝐓,yri​I​𝐓3erfc⁡(κ​ri​I​𝐓)​ri​I​𝐓,x​ri​I​𝐓,zri​I​𝐓3).\nabla_{i}Q_{Ix}=-\sum_{\mathbf{T}}Z_{I}\begin{pmatrix}\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\kappa r_{iI\mathbf{T}})r_{iI\mathbf{T},x}^{2}}{r_{iI\mathbf{T}}^{3}}-\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\kappa r_{iI\mathbf{T}})}{r_{iI\mathbf{T}}}-\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{\pi}}\mathrm{Ei}(-\kappa^{2}r_{iI\mathbf{T}}^{2})\\[10.76385pt] \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\kappa r_{iI\mathbf{T}})r_{iI\mathbf{T},x}r_{iI\mathbf{T},y}}{r_{iI\mathbf{T}}^{3}}\\[10.76385pt] \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\kappa r_{iI\mathbf{T}})r_{iI\mathbf{T},x}r_{iI\mathbf{T},z}}{r_{iI\mathbf{T}}^{3}}\end{pmatrix}. (172)

The Laplacian of QI​βQ_{I\beta} with respect to rir_{i} is obtained by taking the divergence of the above expression, i.e. ∇i2QI​β=∇i⋅∇iQI​β\nabla_{i}^{2}Q_{I\beta}=\nabla_{i}\cdot\nabla_{i}Q_{I\beta}. Carrying out the differentiation analytically, one finds the closed-form expression

∇i2QI​β=−2∑𝐓ZIri​I​𝐓,β[erfc⁡(κ​ri​I​𝐓)ri​I​𝐓3−κπexp⁡(−κ2​ri​I​𝐓2)ri​I​𝐓2].\nabla_{i}^{2}Q_{I\beta}=-2\sum_{\mathbf{T}}Z_{I}r_{iI\mathbf{T},\beta}\left[\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\kappa r_{iI\mathbf{T}})}{r_{iI\mathbf{T}}^{3}}-\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{\pi}}\frac{\exp(-\kappa^2 r_{iI\mathbf{T}}^2)}{r_{iI\mathbf{T}}^{2}}\right]. (173)

While not directly provided in the aforementioned paper, the associated 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-function components are given by

QI​β​(𝐫)=ZI​∑i∑𝐓ri​I​𝐓,β​(erfc⁡(κ​ri​I​𝐓)ri​I​𝐓+κπ​Ei​(−κ2​ri​I​𝐓2)),Q_{I\beta}(\mathbf{r})=Z_{I}\sum_{i}\sum_{\mathbf{T}}r_{iI\mathbf{T},\beta}\left(\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\kappa r_{iI\mathbf{T}})}{r_{iI\mathbf{T}}}+\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{\pi}}\mathrm{Ei}(-\kappa^{2}r_{iI\mathbf{T}}^{2})\right), (174)

where the exponential integral (Ei) term is an extra contribution that is absent in our definition of the 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-function (which only involves the first term).
